title: DC2026: 18th International Symposium on Dendritic Cells
text:
This meeting will promote scientific progress in dendritic cell biology, which is essential for improving immunity
to infections and enhancing vaccine and immunotherapy development. By fostering collaboration and training, it
supports research central to NIAID’s mission to prevent and treat infectious and immune-mediated diseases.

title: Optic neuropathy in familial dysautonomia: determination of disease mechanisms and functional rescue.
text:
We seek to identify the most effective therapeutic approach to rescue visual function in a mouse model of a
severe neurodegenerative disease known as Familial Dysautonomia (FD). Moreover, we will use transcriptomics
at single-cell resolution to investigate the molecular mechanism behind selective retinal ganglion cell (RGC) loss
in FD. The proposed work is highly translational and will be a critical step toward bringing treatment for vision
loss in FD patients.

title: Assessing Urban-Rural Environmental Stress Inequities in ADRD through Ecological Momentary Assessment
text:
This study is about understanding how environmental stress plays a role in the risk of developing Alzheimer’s
disease and related dementias. We focus on comparing the experiences of people living in cities versus those
in rural areas in Indiana, USA, using a mobile app and smartwatch to track their daily stressors and health data.
The goal is to identify specific environmental factors that might contribute to Alzheimer’s and related dementias.

title: Mechanisms of Dynamic Transcriptional Reprogramming in Metastasis Stem Cells
text:
Metastatic cancer cells are able to colonize distant organs, resist therapy and cause cancer death because of
their ability to dynamically change their gene expression programs to adapt to diverse stresses. The molecular
mechanisms of such metastatic plasticity are not understood. Leveraging patient samples, organoids, and
insights we have generated, we will define critical mechanisms of dynamic transcriptional reprogramming in
metastasis, with the potential to impact therapeutic outcomes for patients with metastatic cancer.

title: Understanding disparities in cardiovascular toxicity among breast cancer survivors in Arkansas
text:
Public Health Relevance/Project Narrative Section

Cardiovascular (CV) toxicities from common cancer therapies (trastuzumab, anthracyclines, or left chest radiation) can lead to cardiovascular disease (heart failure, myocardial infarction, and stroke) and are more common in certain breast cancer survivor populations, including individuals living in rural areas or neighborhoods with limited resources. However, it remains unclear how demographic, economic, and geographic factors together influence CV toxicity in breast cancer survivors, and few studies have examined their combined impact on outcomes. This K01 aims to: 1) identify the extent of differences in incident CV toxicity among breast cancer survivors in Arkansas across demographic characteristics, neighborhood economic standing, and geographic contexts; and 2) develop a predictive algorithm for risk stratification in breast cancer survivors at high risk for CV toxicity using machine-learning approaches that incorporate patients’ clinical profiles and community and environmental factors to move beyond describing observed differences in CV toxicities to informing targeted interventions to improve the CV health of breast cancer survivors.

title: Imaging Brain Kappa Opioid Receptors in Early Abstinence Opioid Use Disorder
text:
The kappa opioid receptor (NOR) and the mu opiod receptor (POR) systems are both central to mediating opioid
effects in the brain; yet the overwhelming majority of Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging work in
humans has focused on POR due to the absence of an appropriate PET tracer for NOR. Here, we leverage a
recently developed NOR-selective agonist to for the first time (i) compare the magnitude and regional pattern of
KOR receptor availability between individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD) and healthy controls; (ii) establish
the clinical & transdiagnostic relevance of NOR availability; and (iii) assess the relationship between KOR and
network connectivity using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). The proposed multi-modal and clinical
exploration of this system will fill a current clinical research gap of this potential treatment target.

title: Novel role of ROCK2 in Immune Mechanisms of Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy
text:
Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy is a life-threatening condition with increasing prevalence and associated with
increased cardiovascular risk after a Takotsubo event. Takotsubo is associated with a robust immune
response, a common feature with hypertension, the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease.
These studies aim to determine the mechanisms by with the enzyme ROCK2 functions in myeloid cells to
promote cardiac dysfunction in Takotsubo and how it may promote post-Takotsubo cardiovascular risk in order
to identify novel therapeutic strategies.

title: Senior Research Career Scientist
text:
Dr. Ronald J. Triolo is a Senior Research Career Scientist in the RR&D Service of the US Department of
Veterans Affairs, and a Tenured Full Professor of Biomedical Engineering at Case Western Reserve
University. He is Executive Director of the RR&D Center for Advanced Platform Technology where he
collaborates on the development and translation of novel rehabilitation, assistive or restorative technologies for
individuals with sensorimotor impairments or limb loss. He directs the Motion Study Laboratory of the Louis
Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center where he pursues research in the biomechanics and control of human
movement, and the design and clinical application neural interfaces FOR motor or sensory neuroprostheses.
Dr. Triolo has mentored >40 graduate/medical students and post-doctoral trainees, and authored >150 peer-
reviewed papers/book chapters. He currently leads VA, NIH and DoD funded studies to restore independent
upright/seated mobility, enhance posture and balance, and promote overall health through exercise.

title: Defining the association between trisomy 21 and placentation defects
text:
Proper establishment of a functional placenta is integral to the short and long-term health of a person. People
with Down’s Syndrome develop abnormal placentas and are coincidentally at an increased risk for chronic
diseases that are closely associated with placental insufficiency. We hypothesize gene expression is altered in
Down syndrome placentation and aim to clarify the mechanisms that account for corresponding placental
defects.

title: Understanding HIV-1 persistence in cytotoxic CD4+ T lymphocytes at the single cell level
text:
Despite effective antiretroviral therapy, HIV-1 persists in cytotoxic CD4+ T lymphocytes and survives viral
cytopathic effects and immune clearance. Using single-cell multi-omics profiling, we will examine how antigen
responses and cytokine stimulation promote the persistence of HIV-1-infected, clonally expanding, cytotoxic
CD4+ T cells. Our study will identity immune programs that drive HIV-1 persistence and guide HIV-1
eradication strategies.

title: Computational Modeling Core
text:
Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans are both organisms that are commonly found on healthy
individuals without causing problems but lead to deadly infections in some. The Computational & Predictive
Modeling Core will lead the development of new computational algorithms for pattern matching across
datasets, to identify commonalities across different types of measurements and between both types of
infections. Doing so will improve our ability to predict the outcome of infection and our understanding of how
these infections become life-threatening.

title: The role of endogenous chimeric mRNA encoded GasderminD fusion proteins in immunity
text:
This research will unveil an entirely new mechanism of immune regulation through the formation of endogenous
chimeric mRNA, which generate novel gasdermin fusion proteins that control inflammatory cell death. By
revealing how this RNA-based variation shapes host defense and inflammation, the project will provide
fundamental insights into immune cell biology and inflammatory disease. In the long term, these discoveries
could inform new therapeutic strategies for infectious diseases, sepsis, inflammatory bowel disease, and other
immune-mediated conditions, ultimately helping to reduce illness and improve health outcomes.

title: High-throughput, Multiscale Imaging Spatial Metabolomics
text:
This research program aims to develop next-generation magnetic resonance (MR) and mass
spectrometry (MS)-based spatial metabolomics technologies that will significantly enhance resolution,
sensitivity, throughput, multi-scale integration and temporal characterization. The proposed efforts will
focus on three innovative directions: an intelligent mass spectrometry imaging system integrating AI-
powered adaptive sampling with advanced signal reconstruction, a novel framework (CRISP) that
achieves cell-resolved tissue metabolomic imaging by fusing cell-specific metabolomic codes with
tissue-level data, and a longitudinal dietary isotope labeling method combined with multimodal MR/MS-
based metabolomic imaging to reveal spatiotemporal metabolic dynamics over extended periods.
Successful development of these technologies will transform our ability to characterize biochemical
mechanisms across multiple spatial and temporal scales, ultimately contributing to fundamental
metabolic research and providing new insights into the relationships between spatial metabolic
heterogeneity and biological functions in both healthy and disease states.

title: Population-Based Characterization of Metabolic Pathways to Predict Pediatric Crohn's Disease Outcomes
text: Pediatric Crohn’s Disease (CD) patient populations with severe disease subtypes suffer a loss of structural integrity of the small bowel and/or are non-responsive to treatment, which can negatively impact growth and development in these children. Identification of biomarkers aside from genomics, such as metabolic shifts which may occur in the bowel prior to development of severe disease, hold the power to separate at-risk pediatric populations and help physicians intervene earlier with personalized treatment. In this proposal, we will use a novel computational approach to characterize shifts in metabolism that occur across pediatric CD subtypes leveraging existing data archives with validation within a large prospective cohort of patients from multiple sites in the United States.

title: Structural and functional studies of the mycobacterial transcription cycle
text:
We propose to characterize the transcription cycle structurally and functionally in the
actinobacteria phylum, focusing on the pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis. RNA polymerase,
the central enzyme of transcription, is a proven target for antimicrobials, and regulators of the
transcription cycle are often clade-specific but essential for viability and virulence. Understanding
how these factors regulate Mycobacterium tuberculosis RNA polymerase informs us on unified
and clade-specific mechanisms, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the
transcription cycle that can lead to new therapeutics against specific bacterial pathogens.

title: CranioRate: An imaging-based, deep-phenotyping analysis toolset, repository, and online clinician interface for craniosynostosis
text:
This grant proposal aims to improve our understanding of craniosynostosis by expanding on our prior
work using machine learning methodologies to objectively quantify the head shape anomalies in this
condition. During the project, we will further develop a point-of-care tool, CranioRate™, to allow
physicians to improve their understanding of their patients and create an accessible collection of
imaging data so researchers can more easily study this challenging population of patients. With this
information, surgeons will be able to better tailor their interventions to the needs of their individual
patients, and researchers will improve their understanding of this complex disorder.

title: CHI3L1-Targeted Small Molecules for Glioblastoma
text:
There is an urgent need for the establishment of new immunomodulatory approaches to reverse immune
suppression in glioblastoma. The focus of this work is to validate a new therapeutic strategy for glioblastoma
based on small molecule-based inhibition of a key immunosuppressive pathway. Optimized inhibitors from this
work may synergize with immune checkpoint inhibitors to effectively promote tumor regression for glioblastoma
patients.

title: Lymph Node Digital Twins for Predictive Pharmacology and Target Validation in HIV
text:
Viral persistence in lymph nodes remains a barrier to curing HIV, because variable lymph node size hinders
antiretroviral therapy (ART) penetration, enabling viral persistence despite ongoing therapy. Inflammation during
HIV infection alters lymph node structure and changes drug penetration, but these geometric effects are poorly
defined. We will use 3D-reconstructed simian lymph nodes and machine learning to create digital twins for
population pharmacokinetic studies; these models will clarify how inflammation-driven geometric changes
influence ART distribution, improving our ability to design therapeutic strategies that target lymph node reservoirs
and work toward a cure for HIV.

title: Machine Learning-Driven Precision Dosing System for Improved Anticoagulation Therapy
text:
Warfarin remains a vital anticoagulant for nearly two million Americans, but half of all patients spend significant
time outside the safe therapeutic range, leading to avoidable strokes, bleeding events, hospitalizations, and
billions in annual healthcare costs. This project will develop and validate an adaptive, machine learning–driven
dosing platform that integrates lifestyle, clinical, and pharmacogenomic data to provide precise,
provider-guided dosing recommendations in real time. By improving safety, effectiveness, and accessibility of
warfarin therapy, this innovation has the potential to reduce preventable adverse events, improve outcomes
across diverse patient populations, and lower the economic burden of anticoagulation management.

title: Systems Biophysics of Multiscale State Transitions in Cells and Tissue
text:
This research program aims to advance multiscale biofabrication methods to engineer physiologically
realistic tissues and mini-organs using fully physiological materials, particularly natural, unmodified extracellular
matrix (ECM) solutions such as collagen I, to enhance biomimicry and bioactivity. By applying these techniques,
we will investigate how complex biophysical signals, including ECM architectural cues, drive critical state
transitions across multiple biological scales in both tumor tissues and stem cell-derived tissues, influencing
disease progression and tissue development. The overarching goal is to establish ultra-realistic in vitro tissue
systems that enable a deeper understanding of mechanobiological processes, with broad implications for
regenerative medicine, disease modeling, and therapeutic development.
